Load the data file

The data is from https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1AZvf5EuWStJ-gfY8z_AKUS2i5lRqNUyYWuTTx-pJe2Y/edit?gid=0#gid=0

Make a histogram of the Weight of the students

# With R base
hist(ieap2025$Weight,
     main = "Histogram of the Weight of the students",
     xlab = "Weight (kg)",
     col = "lightblue",
     border = "black",
     breaks = 10)  # nombre de classes

# With ggplot2
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(ieap2025, aes(x = Weight)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 2, fill = "lightblue", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Weight",
       x = "Weight (kg)",
       y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

# With R base
ggplot(ieap2025, aes(x = Weight)) +
  geom_density(fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Density Plot of Weight",
       x = "Weight (kg)",
       y = "Density") +
  theme_minimal()

# With R base
boxplot(ieap2025$Weight,
        main = "Boxplot of Weight",
        ylab = "Weight (kg)",
        col = "orange",
        border = "black")

# With ggplot2
ggplot(ieap2025, aes(y = Weight)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "orange", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Boxplot of Weight",
       y = "Weight (kg)") +
  theme_minimal()

### 3.3 Boxplot to summarize the distribution

  • Main elements of a boxplot:
    • Median (Q2) → line inside the box
    • First quartile (Q1, 25th percentile) → bottom edge of the box
    • Third quartile (Q3, 75th percentile) → top edge of the box
    • Interquartile range (IQR = Q3 − Q1) → spread of the middle 50% of data
    • Whiskers → extend to smallest/largest values within 1.5 × IQR
    • Outliers → points beyond the whiskers
  • Why start with a boxplot for an unknown distribution:
    • Summarizes key statistics (median, quartiles, spread, extremes)
    • Shows asymmetry or skewness in the data
    • Detects potential outliers
    • Compact summary suitable for small or large datasets
    • Requires no assumptions about the distribution (robust for unknown distributions)
  • References for further reading:
    • Boxplot – Wikipedia
    • Understanding Boxplots – Towards Data Science
    • R Boxplot Documentation

# 4. Ask real questions as a scientist.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(ieap2025, aes(x = Gender, y = Weight, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Weight Distribution by Gender",
       x = "Gender",
       y = "Weight (kg)") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("M" = "blue", "F" = "pink")) +
  theme_minimal()

# Explanations about the distribution :

1️⃣ Male vs Female distribution comparison.

Males slightly heavier on average, but overall distributions are similar.

2️⃣ Professional Graph

Boxplot with individual points by gender: shows median, quartiles, outliers, and spread. Improve analysis (on my mind). Use distinct colors for more readability : blue for males and pink for females (quite stereotypics but easy to understand).

3️⃣ Ideal Graph

Fore me, a graph needs to be clear, readable and informative. A histogram can show overall shape, but is less precise for comparing groups.

4️⃣ Let’s try to plot an histogram and decide what is prefered ! # Make a histogram of the Weight separating Males and Females

# Histogram of weight distribution by gender

ggplot(ieap2025, aes(x = Weight, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_histogram(position = "identity", alpha = 0.6, bins = 20, color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Weight by Gender",
       x = "Weight (kg)",
       y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("M" = "blue", "F" = "pink"))

Works but boxplot is preferred for comparing male vs female distributions.

4.1 Is the weight of males/females significantly different?

library(tidyverse)

# Boxplot with points
ggplot(ieap2025, aes(x = Gender, y = Weight, fill = Gender)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Weight Distribution by Gender",
       x = "Gender",
       y = "Weight (kg)") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("M" = "blue", "F" = "pink")) +
  theme_minimal()

# t-test comparing male vs female weights
t_test_result <- t.test(Weight ~ Gender, data = ieap2025)
t_test_result
## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  Weight by Gender
## t = -2.9133, df = 9.8792, p-value = 0.01566
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group F and group M is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  -21.638713  -2.866049
## sample estimates:
## mean in group F mean in group M 
##        60.71429        72.96667
# Calculate effect size (r) from t-test
t_value <- t_test_result$statistic
df <- t_test_result$parameter
r <- sqrt(t_value^2 / (t_value^2 + df))

# Automatic conclusion based on p-value
if(t_test_result$p.value < 0.05){
  cat("Conclusion: There is a statistically significant difference between male and female weights (p =", round(t_test_result$p.value,3), 
      "), and the effect of gender is large (r =", round(r,2), ").\n")
} else {
  cat("Conclusion: There is no statistically significant difference between male and female weights (p =", round(t_test_result$p.value,3), ").\n")
}
## Conclusion: There is a statistically significant difference between male and female weights (p = 0.016 ), and the effect of gender is large (r = 0.68 ).
